entries.c0c95f0b6a5e23f59932fa16116496913c4c6b3c: <div sID="gen9475" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Job.11" sID="Job.11"/> <div eID="gen9475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9476" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9477" type="x-p"/> Poor Job's wound's were yet bleeding, his sore still runs and ceases not, but none of his friends bring him any oil, any balm; Zophar, the third, pours into them as much vinegar as the two former had done. I. He exhibits a very high charge against Job, as proud and false in justifying himself, <reference osisRef="Job.11.1-Job.11.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He appeals to God for his conviction, and begs that God would take him to task (<reference osisRef="Job.11.5">ver. 5</reference>) and that Job might be made sensible, 1. Of God's unerring wisdom and his inviolable justice, <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">ver. 6</reference>. 2. Of his unsearchable perfections, <reference osisRef="Job.11.7-Job.11.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. 3. Of his incontestable sovereignty and uncontrollable power, <reference osisRef="Job.11.10">ver. 10</reference>. 4. Of the cognizance he takes of the children of men, <reference osisRef="Job.11.11-Job.11.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. III. He assures him that, upon his repentance and reformation (<reference osisRef="Job.11.13-Job.11.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>), God would restore him to his former prosperity and safety (<reference osisRef="Job.11.15-Job.11.19">ver. 15-19</reference>); but that, if he were wicked it was in vain to expect it, <reference osisRef="Job.11.20">ver. 20</reference>.
entries.b42162b80459b132226149717bb8e60db744c755: <div eID="gen9477" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9476" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Zophar. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9478" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said, 2 Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified? <hi type="super">3</hi> Should thy lies make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest, shall no man make thee ashamed? <hi type="super">4</hi> For thou hast said, My doctrine <hi type="italic">is</hi> pure, and I am clean in thine eyes. <hi type="super">5</hi> But oh that God would speak, and open his lips against thee; <hi type="super">6</hi> And that he would show thee the secrets of wisdom, that <hi type="italic">they are</hi> double to that which is! Know therefore that God exacteth of thee <hi type="italic">less</hi> than thine iniquity <hi type="italic">deserveth.</hi> <div eID="gen9478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9479" type="x-p"/> It is sad to see what intemperate passions even wise and good men are sometimes betrayed into by the heat of disputation, of which Zophar here is an instance. Eliphaz began with a very modest preface, <reference osisRef="Job.4.2">ch. iv. 2</reference>. Bildad was a little more rough upon Job, <reference osisRef="Job.8.2">ch. viii. 2</reference>. But Zophar falls upon him without mercy, and gives him very bad language: <hi type="italic">Should a man full of talk be justified? And should thy lies make men hold their peace?</hi> Is this the way to comfort Job? No, nor to convince him neither. Does this become one that appears as an advocate for God and his justice? <hi type="italic">Tantæne animis coelestibus iræ?—In heavenly breasts can such resentment dwell?</hi> Those that engage in controversy will find it very hard to keep their temper. All the wisdom, caution, and resolution they have will be little enough to prevent their breaking out into such indecencies as we here find Zophar guilty of. <div eID="gen9479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9480" type="x-p"/> I. He represents Job otherwise than what he was, <reference osisRef="Job.11.2-Job.11.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He would have him thought idle and impertinent in his discourse, and one that loved to hear himself talk; he gives him the lie, and calls him <hi type="italic">a mocker;</hi> and all this that it might be looked upon as a piece of justice to chastise him. Those that have a mind to fall out with their brethren, and to fall foul upon them, find it necessary to put the worst colours they can upon them and their performances, and, right or wrong, to make them odious. We have read and considered Job's discourses in the foregoing chapters, and have found them full of good sense and much to the purpose, that his principles are right, his reasonings strong, many of his expressions weighty and very considerable, and that what there is in them of heat and passion a little candour and charity will excuse and overlook; and yet Zophar here invidiously represents him, 1. As a man that never considered what he said, but uttered what came uppermost, only to make a noise with the multitude of words, hoping by that means to carry his cause and run down his reprovers: <hi type="italic">Should not the multitude of words be answered?</hi> Truly, sometimes it is no great matter whether it be or no; silence perhaps is the best confutation of impertinence and puts the greatest contempt upon it. <hi type="italic">Answer not a fool according to his folly.</hi> But, if it be answered, let reason and grace have the answering of it, not pride and passion. <hi type="italic">Should a man full of talk</hi> (margin, <hi type="italic">a man of lips,</hi> that is all tongue, <hi type="italic">vox et præterea nihil—mere voice</hi>) <hi type="italic">be justified?</hi> Should he be justified in his loquacity, as in effect he is if he be not reproved for it? No, for <hi type="italic">in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin.</hi> Should he be justified by it? Shall many words pass for valid pleas? Shall he carry the day with the flourishes of language? No, he shall not be accepted with God, or any wise men, <hi type="italic">for his much speaking,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.7">Matt. vi. 7</reference>. 2. As a man that made no conscience of what he said—a liar, and one that hoped by the impudence of lies to silence his adversaries (<hi type="italic">should thy lies make men hold their peace?</hi>)—a mocker, one that bantered all mankind, and knew how to put false colours upon any thing, and was not ashamed to impose upon every one that talked with him: <hi type="italic">When thou mockest shall no man make thee ashamed?</hi> Is it not time to speak, to stem such a violent tide as this? Job was not mad, but spoke the words of truth and soberness, and yet was thus misrepresented. Eliphaz and Bildad had answered him, and said what they could to make him ashamed; it was therefore no instance of Zophar's generosity to set upon a man so violently who was already thus harassed. Here were three matched against one. <div eID="gen9480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9481" type="x-p"/> II. He charges Job with saying that which he had not said (<reference osisRef="Job.11.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast said, My doctrine is pure.</hi> And what if he had said so? It was true that Job was sound in the faith, and orthodox in his judgment, and spoke better of God than his friends did. If he had expressed himself unwarily, yet it did not therefore follow but that his doctrine was true. But he charges him with saying, <hi type="italic">I am clean in thy eyes.</hi> Job had not said so: he had indeed said, <hi type="italic">Thou knowest that I am not wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.10.7">ch. x. 7</reference>); but he had also said, <hi type="italic">I have sinned,</hi> and never pretended to a spotless perfection. He had indeed maintained that he was not a hypocrite as they charged him; but to infer thence that he would not own himself a sinner was an unfair insinuation. We ought to put the best construction on the words and actions of our brethren that they will bear; but contenders are tempted to put the worst. <div eID="gen9481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9482" type="x-p"/> III. He appeals to God, and wishes him to appear against Job. So very confident is he that Job is in the wrong that nothing will serve him but that God must immediately appear to silence and condemn him. We are commonly ready with too much assurance to interest God in our quarrels, and to conclude that, if he would but speak, he would take our part and speak for us, as Zophar here: <hi type="italic">O that God would speak!</hi> for he would certainly <hi type="italic">open his lips against thee;</hi> whereas, when God did speak, he opened his lips for Job against his three friends. We ought indeed to leave all controversies to be determined by the judgment of God, which we are sure <hi type="italic">is according to truth;</hi> but those are not always in the right who are most forward to appeal to that judgment and prejudge it against their antagonists. Zophar despairs to convince Job himself, and therefore desires God would convince him of two things which it is good for every one of us duly to consider, and under all our afflictions cheerfully to confess:— <div eID="gen9482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9483" type="x-p"/> 1. The unsearchable depth of God's counsels. Zophar cannot pretend to do it, but he desires that God himself would show Job so much of the secrets of the divine wisdom as might convince him that <hi type="italic">they are at least double to that which is,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, (1.) There are secrets in the divine wisdom, <hi type="italic">arcana imperii—state-secrets.</hi> God's way is in the sea. Clouds and darkness are round about him. He has reasons of state which we cannot fathom and must not pry into. (2.) What we know of God is nothing to what we cannot know. What is hidden is more than double to what appears, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>. (3.) By employing ourselves in adoring the depth of those divine counsels of which we cannot find the bottom we shall very much tranquilize our minds under the afflicting hand of God. (4.) God knows a great deal more evil of us than we do of ourselves; so some understand it. When God gave David a sight and sense of sin he said that he had <hi type="italic">in the hidden part made him to know wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Ps. li. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen9483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9484" type="x-p"/> 2. The unexceptionable justice of his proceedings. "Know therefore that, how sore soever the correction is that thou art under, <hi type="italic">God exacteth of thee less than thy iniquity deserves,</hi>" or (as some read it), "he <hi type="italic">remits thee part of thy iniquity,</hi> and does not deal with thee according to the full demerit of it." Note, (1.) When the debt of duty is not paid it is justice to insist upon the debt of punishment. (2.) Whatever punishment is inflicted upon us in this world we must own that it is less than our iniquities deserve, and therefore, instead of complaining of our troubles, we must be thankful that we are out of hell, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">Lam. iii. 39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.10">Ps. ciii. 10</reference>.
entries.f97eb02c519643ad95efa21fe64cae9aafb6e23e: <div eID="gen9484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9485" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know? <hi type="super">9</hi> The measure thereof <hi type="italic">is</hi> longer than the earth, and broader than the sea. <hi type="super">10</hi> If he cut off, and shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him? <hi type="super">11</hi> For he knoweth vain men: he seeth wickedness also; will he not then consider <hi type="italic">it?</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> For vain man would be wise, though man be born <hi type="italic">like</hi> a wild ass's colt. <div eID="gen9485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9486" type="x-p"/> Zophar here speaks very good things concerning God and his greatness and glory, concerning man and his vanity and folly: these two compared together, and duly considered, will have a powerful influence upon our submission to all the dispensations of the divine Providence. <div eID="gen9486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9487" type="x-p"/> I. See here what God is, and let him be adored. <div eID="gen9487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9488" type="x-p"/> 1. He is an incomprehensible Being, infinite and immense, whose nature and perfections our finite understandings cannot possibly form any adequate conceptions of, and whose counsels and actings we cannot therefore, without the greatest presumption, pass a judgment upon. We that are so little acquainted with the divine nature are incompetent judges of the divine providence; and, when we censure the dispensations of it, we talk of things that we do not understand. We cannot find out God; how dare we then find fault with him? Zophar here shows, (1.) That God's nature infinitely exceeds the capacities of our understandings: "<hi type="italic">Canst thou find out God, find him out to perfection?</hi> No, <hi type="italic">What canst thou do? What canst thou know?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.11.7-Job.11.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Thou, a poor, weak, short-sighted creature, a worm of the earth, that art but of yesterday? Thou, though ever so inquisitive after him, ever so desirous and industrious to find him out, yet darest thou attempt the search, or canst thou hope to speed in it? We may, by searching find God (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.27">Acts xvii. 27</reference>), but we cannot find him out in any thing he is pleased to conceal; we may apprehend him, but we cannot comprehend him; we may know that he is, but cannot know what he is. The eye can see the ocean but not see over it. We may, by a humble, diligent, and believing search, find out something of God, but cannot find him out to perfection; we may know, but cannot know fully, what God is, nor find out his work <hi type="italic">from the beginning to the end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Eccl. iii. 11</reference>. Note, God is unsearchable. The ages of his eternity cannot be numbered, nor the spaces of his immensity measured; the depths of his wisdom cannot be fathomed, nor the reaches of his power bounded; the brightness of his glory can never be described, nor the treasures of his goodness reckoned up. This is a good reason why we should always speak of God with humility and caution and never prescribe to him nor quarrel with him, why we should be thankful for what he has revealed of himself and long to be where we shall see him as he is, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.9-1Cor.13.10">1 Cor. xiii. 9, 10</reference>. (2.) That it infinitely exceeds the limits of the whole creation: <hi type="italic">It is higher than heaven</hi> (so some read it), <hi type="italic">deeper than hell,</hi> the great abyss, <hi type="italic">longer than the earth, and broader than the sea,</hi> many parts of which are to this day undiscovered, and more were then. It is quite out of our reach to comprehend God's nature. <hi type="italic">Such knowledge is too wonderful for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Ps. cxxxix. 6</reference>. We cannot fathom God's designs, nor find out the reasons of his proceedings. His judgments are a great deep. Paul attributes such immeasurable dimensions to the divine love as Zophar here attributes to the divine wisdom, and yet recommends it to our acquaintance. <reference osisRef="Eph.3.18-Eph.3.19">Eph. iii. 18, 19</reference>, <hi type="italic">That you may know the breadth, and length, and depth, and height, of the love of Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen9488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9489" type="x-p"/> 2. God is a sovereign Lord (<reference osisRef="Job.11.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">If he cut off</hi> by death (margin, <hi type="italic">If he make a change,</hi> for death is a change; if he make a change in nations, in families, in the posture of our affairs),—if he <hi type="italic">shut up</hi> in prison, or in the net of affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.11">Ps. lxvi. 11</reference>),—if he seize any creature as a hunter his prey, he will gather it (so bishop Patrick) and who shall force him to restore? or if he <hi type="italic">gather together,</hi> as tares for the fire, or <hi type="italic">if he gather to himself man's spirit and breath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.34.14">ch. xxxiv. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">then who can hinder him?</hi> Who can either arrest the sentence or oppose the execution? Who can control his power or arraign his wisdom and justice? If he that made all out of nothing think fit to reduce all to nothing, or to their first chaos again,—if he that separated between light and darkness, dry land and sea, at first, please to gather them together again,—if he that made unmakes, <hi type="italic">who can turn him away,</hi> alter his mind or stay his hand, impede or impeach his proceedings? <div eID="gen9489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9490" type="x-p"/> 3. God is a strict and just observer of the children of men (<reference osisRef="Job.11.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">He knows vain men.</hi> We know little of him, but he knows us perfectly: <hi type="italic">He sees wickedness also,</hi> not to approve it (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab. i. 13</reference>), but to animadvert upon it. (1.) He observes vain men. Such all are (<hi type="italic">every man, at his best estate, is altogether vanity</hi>), and he considers it in his dealings with them. He knows what the projects and hopes of vain men are, and can blast and defeat them, the workings of their foolish fancies; he sits in heaven, and laughs at them. He takes knowledge of the vanity of men (that is, their little sins; so some) their vain thoughts and vain words, and unsteadiness in that which is good. (2.) He observes bad men: <hi type="italic">He sees</hi> gross <hi type="italic">wickedness also,</hi> though committed ever so secretly and ever so artfully palliated and disguised. All the wickedness of the wicked is naked and open before the all-seeing eye of God: <hi type="italic">Will he not then consider it?</hi> Yes, certainly he will, and will reckon for it, though for a time he seem to keep silence. <div eID="gen9490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9491" type="x-p"/> II. See here what man is, and let him be humbled, <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">v. 12</reference>. God sees this concerning vain man that he <hi type="italic">would be wise,</hi> would be thought so, <hi type="italic">though he is born like a wild ass's colt,</hi> so sottish and foolish, unteachable and untameable. See what man is. 1. He is a vain creature—<hi type="italic">empty;</hi> so the word is. God made him full, but he emptied himself, impoverished himself, and now he is <hi type="italic">raca,</hi> a creature that has nothing in him. 2. He is a foolish creature, has become <hi type="italic">like the beasts that perish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">Ps. xlix. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.22">lxxiii. 22</reference>), an idiot, born like an ass, the most stupid animal, an ass's colt, not yet brought to any service. If ever he come to be good for any thing, it is owing to the grace of Christ, who once, in the day of his triumph, served himself by an ass's colt. 3. He is a wilful ungovernable creature. An ass's colt may be made good for something, but the wild ass's colt will never be reclaimed, nor regards the crying of the driver. See <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.39.7">Job xxxix. 5-7</reference>. Man thinks himself as much at liberty, and his own master, as the wild ass's colt does, that is <hi type="italic">used to the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jer. ii. 24</reference>), eager to gratify his own appetites and passions. 4. Yet he is a proud creature and self-conceited. He <hi type="italic">would be wise,</hi> would he thought so, values himself upon the honour of wisdom, though he will not submit to the laws of wisdom. He would be wise, that is, he reaches after forbidden wisdom, and, like his first parents, aiming to be wise above what is written, loses the tree of life for the tree of knowledge. Now is such a creature as this fit to contend with God or call him to an account? Did we but better know God and ourselves, we should better know how to conduct ourselves towards God.
entries.f0733a85a006600fb230a5550a6c6104b0ee155e: <div eID="gen9491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him; <hi type="super">14</hi> If iniquity <hi type="italic">be</hi> in thine hand, put it far away, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacles. <hi type="super">15</hi> For then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; yea, thou shalt be stedfast, and shalt not fear: <hi type="super">16</hi> Because thou shalt forget <hi type="italic">thy</hi> misery, <hi type="italic">and</hi> remember <hi type="italic">it</hi> as waters <hi type="italic">that</hi> pass away: <hi type="super">17</hi> And <hi type="italic">thine</hi> age shall be clearer than the noonday; thou shalt shine forth, thou shalt be as the morning. <hi type="super">18</hi> And thou shalt be secure, because there is hope; yea, thou shalt dig <hi type="italic">about thee, and</hi> thou shalt take thy rest in safety. <hi type="super">19</hi> Also thou shalt lie down, and none shall make <hi type="italic">thee</hi> afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and they shall not escape, and their hope <hi type="italic">shall be as</hi> the giving up of the ghost. <div eID="gen9492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9493" type="x-p"/> Zophar, as the other two, here encourages Job to hope for better times if he would but come to a better temper. <div eID="gen9493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9494" type="x-p"/> I. He gives him good counsel (<reference osisRef="Job.11.13-Job.11.14">v. 13, 14</reference>), as Eliphaz did (<reference osisRef="Job.5.8">ch. v. 8</reference>), and Bildad, <reference osisRef="Job.8.5">ch. viii. 5</reference>. He would have him repent and return to God. Observe the steps of that return. 1. He must look within, and get his mind changed and the tree made good. He must <hi type="italic">prepare his heart;</hi> there the work of conversion and reformation must begin. The heart that wandered from God must be reduced—that was defiled with sin and put into disorder must be cleansed and put in order again—that was wavering and unfixed must be settled and established; so the word here signifies. The heart is then prepared to seek God when it is determined and fully resolved to make a business of it and to go through with it. 2. He must look up, and <hi type="italic">stretch out his hands towards God,</hi> that is, must stir up himself to take hold on God, must pray to him with earnestness and importunity, striving in prayer, and with expectation to receive mercy and grace from him. To <hi type="italic">give the hand to the Lord</hi> signifies to yield ourselves to him and to covenant with him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.8">2 Chron. xxx. 8</reference>. This Job must do, and, for the doing of it, must prepare his heart. Job had prayed, but Zophar would have him to pray in a better manner, not as an appellant, but as a petitioner and humble suppliant. 3. He must amend what was amiss in his own conversation, else his prayers would be ineffectual (<reference osisRef="Job.11.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If iniquity be in thy hand</hi> (that is, if there be any sin which thou dost yet live in the practice of) <hi type="italic">put it far away,</hi> forsake it with detestation and a holy indignation, stedfastly resolving not to return to it, nor ever to have any thing more to do with it. <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.31">Ezek. xviii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos. xiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa. xxx. 22</reference>. If any of the gains of iniquity, any goods gotten by fraud or oppression, be in thy hand, make restitution thereof" (as Zaccheus, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.8">Luke xix. 8</reference>), "and <hi type="italic">shake thy hands from holding them,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa. xxxiii. 15</reference>. The guilt of sin is not removed if the gain of sin be not restored. 4. He must do his utmost to reform his family too: "<hi type="italic">Let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacles;</hi> let not thy house harbour or shelter any wicked persons, any wicked practices, or any wealth gotten by wickedness." He suspected that Job's great household had been ill-governed, and that, where there were many, there were many wicked, and the ruin of his family was the punishment of the wickedness of it; and therefore, if he expected God should return to him, he must reform what was amiss there, and, though wickedness might come into his tabernacles, he must not suffer it to dwell there, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3-Ps.101.8">Ps. ci. 3</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen9494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> II. He assures him of comfort if he took this counsel, <reference osisRef="Job.11.15-Job.11.20">v. 15</reference>, &c. If he would repent and reform, he should, without doubt, be easy and happy, and all would be well. Perhaps Zophar might insinuate that, unless God did speedily make such a change as this in his condition, he and his friends would be confirmed in their opinion of him as a hypocrite and a dissembler with God. A great truth, however, is conveyed, That, <hi type="italic">the work of righteousness will be peace, and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa. xxxii. 17</reference>. Those that sincerely turn to God may expect, <div eID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> 1. A holy confidence towards God: "<hi type="italic">Then shalt thou lift up thy face towards heaven</hi> without spot; thou mayest come boldly to the throne of grace, and not with that terror and amazement expressed," <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">ch. ix. 34</reference>. If our hearts condemn us not for hypocrisy and impenitency, then have we confidence in our approaches to God and expectations from him, <reference osisRef="1John.3.21">1 John iii. 21</reference>. If we are looked upon in the face of the anointed, our faces, that were dejected, may be lifted up—that were polluted, being washed with the blood of Christ, may be lifted up without spot. We may <hi type="italic">draw near in full assurance of faith</hi> when we are <hi type="italic">sprinkled from an evil conscience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">Heb. x. 22</reference>. Some understand this of the clearing up of his credit before men, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.6">Ps. xxxvii. 6</reference>. If we make our peace with God, we may with cheerfulness look our friends in the face. <div eID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9497" type="x-p"/> 2. A holy composedness in themselves: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be stedfast, and shalt not fear,</hi> not <hi type="italic">be afraid of evil tidings,</hi> thy heart being fixed, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.7">Ps. cxii. 7</reference>. Job was now full of confusion (<reference osisRef="Job.10.15">ch. x. 15</reference>), while he looked upon God as his enemy and quarrelled with him; but Zophar assures him that, if he would submit and humble himself, his mind would be composed, and he would be freed from those frightful apprehensions he had of God, which put him into such an agitation. The less we are frightened the more we are fixed, and consequently the more fit we are for our services and for our sufferings. <div eID="gen9497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9498" type="x-p"/> 3. A comfortable reflection upon their past troubles (<reference osisRef="Job.11.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt forget thy misery,</hi> as the mother forgets her travailing pains, for joy that the child is born; thou shalt be perfectly freed from the impressions it makes upon thee, and <hi type="italic">thou shalt remember it as waters that pass away,</hi> or are poured out of a vessel, which leave no taste or tincture behind them, as other liquors do. The wounds of thy present affliction shall be perfectly healed, not only without a remaining scar, but without a remaining pain." Job had endeavoured to forget his complaint (<reference osisRef="Job.9.27">ch. ix. 27</reference>), but found he could not; his soul <hi type="italic">had still in remembrance the wormwood and the gall:</hi> but here Zophar puts him in a way to forget it; let him by faith and prayer bring his griefs and cares to God, an leave them with him, and then he shall forget them. Where sin sits heavily affliction sits lightly. If we duly remember our sins, we shall, in comparison with them, forget our misery, much more if we obtain the comfort of a sealed pardon and a settled peace. He whose iniquity is forgiven shall <hi type="italic">not say, I am sick,</hi> but shall forget his sickness, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa. xxxiii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen9498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9499" type="x-p"/> 4. A comfortable prospect of their future peace. This Zophar here thinks to please Job with, in answer to the many despairing expressions he had used, as if it were to no purpose for him to hope ever to see good days again in this world: "Yea, but thou mayest" (says Zophar) "and good nights too." A blessed change he here puts him in hopes of. <div eID="gen9499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9500" type="x-p"/> (1.) That though now his light was eclipsed it should shine out again, and more brightly than ever (<reference osisRef="Job.11.17">v. 17</reference>),—that even his setting sun should out-shine his noon-day sun, and his evening be fair and clear as the morning, in respect both of honour and pleasure.—that his light should shine <hi type="italic">out of obscurity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">Isa. lviii. 10</reference>), and the thick and dark cloud, from behind which his sun should break forth, would serve as a foil to its lustre,—that it should shine even in old age, and those evil days should be good days to him. Note, Those that truly turn to God then begin to shine forth; their path is as the shining light which increases, the period of their day will be the perfection of it, and their evening to this world will be their morning to a better. <div eID="gen9500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9501" type="x-p"/> (2.) That, though now he was in a continual fear and terror, he should live in a holy rest and security, and find himself continually safe and easy (<reference osisRef="Job.11.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be secure, because there is hope.</hi> Note, Those who have a good hope, through grace, in God, and of heaven, are certainly safe, and have reason to be secure, how difficult soever the times are through which they pass in this world. He that walks uprightly may thus walk surely, because, though there are trouble and danger, yet there is hope that all will be well at last. Hope is <hi type="italic">an anchor of the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.19">Heb. vi. 19</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt dig about thee,</hi>" that is, "Thou shalt be as safe as an army in its entrenchments." Those that submit to God's government shall be taken under his protection, and then they are safe both day and night. [1.] By day, when they employ themselves abroad: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt dig in safety,</hi> thou and thy servants for thee, and not be again set upon by the plunderers, who fell upon thy servants at plough," <reference osisRef="Job.1.14-Job.1.15">ch. i. 14, 15</reference>. It is no part of the promised prosperity that he should live in idleness, but that he should have a calling and follow it, and, when he was about the business of it, should be under the divine protection. Thou shalt dig and be safe, not rob and be safe, revel and be safe. The way of duty is the way of safety. [2.] By night, when they repose themselves at home: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt take thy rest</hi> (and <hi type="italic">the sleep of the labouring man is sweet</hi>) <hi type="italic">in safety,</hi> notwithstanding the dangers of the darkness. The pillar of cloud by day shall be a pillar of fire by night: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt lie down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.11.19">v. 19</reference>), not forced to wander where there is no place to lay thy head on, nor forced to watch and sit up in expectation of assaults; but thou shalt go to bed at bedtime, and not only shall non hurt thee, but none shall make thee afraid nor so much as give thee an alarm." Note, It is a great mercy to have quiet nights and undisturbed sleeps; those say so that are within the hearing of the noise of war. And the way to be quiet is to seek unto God and keep ourselves in his love. Nothing needs make those afraid who <hi type="italic">return to God as their rest</hi> and take him for their habitation. <div eID="gen9501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9502" type="x-p"/> (3.) That, though now he was slighted, yet he should be courted: "<hi type="italic">Many shall make suit to thee,</hi> and think it their interest to secure thy friendship." Suit is made to those that are eminently wise or reputed to be so, that are very rich or in power. Zophar knew Job so well that he foresaw that, how low soever this present ebb was, if once the tide turned, it would flow as high as ever; and he would be again the darling of his country. Those that rightly make suit to God will probably see the day when others will make suit to them, as the foolish virgins to the wise, <hi type="italic">Give us of your oil.</hi> <div eID="gen9502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9503" type="x-p"/> III. Zophar concludes with a brief account of the doom of wicked people (<reference osisRef="Job.11.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">But the eyes of the wicked shall fail.</hi> It should seem, he suspected that Job would not take his counsel, and here tells him what would then come of it, setting death as well as life before him. See what will become of those who persist in their wickedness, and will not be reformed. 1. They shall not reach the good they flatter themselves with the hopes of in this world and in the other. Disappointments will be their doom, their shame, their endless torment. Their eyes shall fail with expecting that which will never come. <hi type="italic">When a wicked man dies his expectation perishes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Prov. xi. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their hope shall be as a puff of breath</hi> (margin), vanished and gone past recall. Or their hope will perish and expire as a man does when he gives up the ghost; it will fail them when they have most need of it and when they expected the accomplishment of it; it will die away, and leave them in utter confusion. 2. They shall not avoid the evil which sometimes they frighten themselves with the apprehensions of. They shall not escape the execution of the sentence passed upon them, can neither out-brave it nor outrun it. Those that will not fly to God will find it in vain to think of flying from him.  <chapter eID="Job.11"/> <div eID="gen9503" type="x-p"/>

entries.ec7d3e86fb112af5a44b065714431eed146dc1a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4670"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen6768" type="x-p"/> FIRST SERIES.<div eID="gen6768" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.11.1-Job.11.20">Job 11:1-20</reference>. First Speech of Zophar.</title> <div sID="gen6769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4670"/>2. Zophar assails Job for his empty words, and indirectly, the two friends, for their weak reply. Taciturnity is highly prized among Orientals (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">Pr 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">19</reference>). <div eID="gen6769" type="x-p"/>
entries.b58a877c852ed88410790f40c18841ef690dab80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4671"/><div sID="gen6770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4671"/><hi type="bold">3. lies--</hi>rather, "vain boasting" (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.30">Jr 48:30</reference>). The "men" is emphatic; men of sense; in antithesis to "vain boasting."<div eID="gen6770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mockest--</hi>upbraidest God by complaints, "shall no man make thee ashamed?" <div eID="gen6771" type="x-p"/>
entries.8027e429c7fd56dd162f7c707db6917096e51313: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4672"/><div sID="gen6772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4672"/><hi type="bold">4. doctrine--</hi>purposely used of Job's speeches, which sounded like lessons of doctrine (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.4.2">Pr 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen6772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine--</hi>addressed to God. Job had maintained his sincerity against his friends suspicions, not faultlessness. <div eID="gen6773" type="x-p"/>
entries.15ffbd30f0f8b1e6c1d91673e2c2531c284d1406: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4673"/><div sID="gen6774" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4673"/><hi type="bold">6. to that which is!--</hi>Rather, "they are double to [man's] wisdom" [Michaelis]. So the Hebrew is rendered (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pr 2:7</reference>). God's ways, which you arraign, if you were shown their secret wisdom, would be seen vastly to exceed that of men, including yours (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.25">1Co 1:25</reference>).<div eID="gen6774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exacteth--</hi>Rather, "God consigns to oblivion in thy favor much of thy guilt." <div eID="gen6775" type="x-p"/>
entries.1db25ab199bdb952b3e603418cf688dc765e760a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4674"/><div sID="gen6776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4674"/>7. Rather, "Penetrate to the perfections of the Almighty" (<reference osisRef="Job.9.10">Job 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference>). <div eID="gen6776" type="x-p"/>
entries.a77e8df73ff2db41d8ee5bec0870cda06b43f167: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4675"/><div sID="gen6777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4675"/><hi type="bold">8. It--</hi>the "wisdom" of God (<reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference>). The abruptness of the Hebrew is forcible: "The heights of heaven! What canst thou do" (as to attaining to them with thy gaze, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>)?<div eID="gen6777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know--</hi>namely, of His perfections. <div eID="gen6778" type="x-p"/>
entries.9204835874a241e8b97e0c94b53348f4a5b809a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4676"/><div sID="gen6779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4676"/><hi type="bold">10. cut off--</hi>Rather, as in <reference osisRef="Job.9.11">Job 9:11</reference>, "pass over," as a storm; namely, rush upon in anger.<div eID="gen6779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shut up--</hi>in prison, with a view to trial.<div eID="gen6780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather together--</hi>the parties for judgment: hold a judicial assembly; to pass sentence on the prisoners. <div eID="gen6781" type="x-p"/>
entries.336ef547e55fabc9cc0c62ea84c88d9c848d92b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4677"/><div sID="gen6782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4677"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">Psa 94:11</reference>).<div eID="gen6782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consider--</hi>so as to punish it. Rather, from the connection, <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference>, "He seeth wickedness also, which man does not perceive"; literally, "But no (other, save He) perceiveth it" [Umbreit]. God's "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference>), detects sin where Job's human eye cannot reach (<reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>), so as to see any. <div eID="gen6783" type="x-p"/>
entries.c65bdd926755229c7f2f103bee07e8fbc6cdfbe9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4678"/><div sID="gen6784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4678"/><hi type="bold">12. vain--</hi>hollow.<div eID="gen6784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">would be--</hi>"wants to consider himself wise"; opposed to God's "wisdom" (see on <reference osisRef="Job.11.11">Job 11:11</reference>); refuses to see sin, where God sees it (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.22">Ro 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen6785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wild ass's colt--</hi>a proverb for untamed wildness (<reference osisRef="Job.39.5">Job 39:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.39.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jr 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Ge 16:12</reference>; Hebrew, "a wild-ass man"). Man wishes to appear wisely obedient to his Lord, whereas he is, from his birth, unsubdued in spirit. <div eID="gen6786" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0cb4c47056640a780d5bd3501249f2a66d38c17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4679"/><div sID="gen6787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4679"/>13. The apodosis to the "If" is at <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>. The preparation of the heart is to be obtained (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.1">Pr 16:1</reference>) by stretching out the hands in prayer for it (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Psa 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.18">1Ch 29:18</reference>). <div eID="gen6787" type="x-p"/>
entries.6830a66256629f5da00b151e8985ac415a48cf8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4680"/><div sID="gen6788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4680"/>14. Rather, "if thou wilt put far away the iniquity in thine hand" (as Zaccheus did, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.8">Lu 19:8</reference>). The apodosis or conclusion is at <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>, "then shalt thou," &c. <div eID="gen6788" type="x-p"/>
entries.03a7444925300960ef695a968c66c3125f65c880: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4681"/><div sID="gen6789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4681"/>15. Zophar refers to Job's own words (<reference osisRef="Job.10.15">Job 10:15</reference>), "yet will I not lift up my head," even though righteous. Zophar declares, if Job will follow his advice, he may "lift up his face."<div eID="gen6789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spot--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.5">De 32:5</reference>).<div eID="gen6790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">steadfast--</hi>literally, "run fast together," like metals which become firm and hard by fusion. The sinner on the contrary is wavering. <div eID="gen6791" type="x-p"/>
entries.2382741eff24b5e316eca79d30aae70bb1461fcc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4682"/><div sID="gen6792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4682"/>16. Just as when the stream runs dry (<reference osisRef="Job.6.17">Job 6:17</reference>), the danger threatened by its wild waves is forgotten (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.16">Is 65:16</reference>) [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6792" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2b7a711efb8a6bee79d9dcc0443a4b2ab26093c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4683"/><div sID="gen6793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4683"/><hi type="bold">17. age--</hi>days of life.<div eID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the noon-day--</hi>namely, of thy former prosperity; which, in the poet's image, had gone on increasing, until it reached its height, as the sun rises higher and higher until it reaches the meridian (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shine forth--</hi>rather, "though now in darkness, thou shall be as the morning"; or, "thy darkness (if any dark shade should arise on thee, it) shall be as the morning" (only the dullness of morning twilight, not nocturnal darkness) [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6795" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cca2fa6685fb55a6904a78bb6d86e3b89493bfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4684"/><div sID="gen6796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4684"/>18. The experience of thy life will teach thee there is hope for man in every trial.<div eID="gen6796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dig--</hi>namely, wells; the chief necessity in the East. Better, "though now ashamed (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>, opposed to the previous 'hope'), thou shalt then rest safely" [Gesenius]; <div eID="gen6797" type="x-p"/>
entries.844af6db98c133be136a87bf3cde147901c4987c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4685"/><div sID="gen6798" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4685"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Psa 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.24">Pr 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.30">Is 14:30</reference>); oriental images of prosperity.<div eID="gen6798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make suit--</hi>literally, "stroke thy face," "caress thee" (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.6">Pr 19:6</reference>). <div eID="gen6799" type="x-p"/>
entries.6385d207c9f27e2e70b43e8911b257eaaa46990c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4686"/><div sID="gen6800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4686"/>20. A warning to Job, if he would not turn to God.<div eID="gen6800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The wicked--</hi>that is, obdurate sinners.<div eID="gen6801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes ... fail--</hi>that is, in vain look for relief (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.65">De 28:65</reference>). Zophar implies Job's only hope of relief is in a change of heart.<div eID="gen6802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall not escape--</hi>literally, "every refuge shall vanish from them."<div eID="gen6803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">giving up of the ghost--</hi>Their hope shall leave them as the breath does the body (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Pr 11:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.11"/>

entries.dade2a204637a9e56e45c2d763f34f4d11d939d5: <div eID="gen16327" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16328" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16329" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16329" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16328" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16330" type="x-p"/> Zophar answers Job, and reproves him severely for his attempts to justify himself; charges him with secret iniquity, and contends that God inflicts less punishment on him than his iniquities deserve, <reference osisRef="Job.11.1-Job.11.6">Job 11:1-6</reference>. Shows the knowledge and perfections of God to be unsearchable, and that none can resist his power, <reference osisRef="Job.11.7-Job.11.11">Job 11:7-11</reference>. Warns him against vanity of mind, and exhorts him to repentance on the ground that his acceptance with God is still a possible case, and that his latter days may yet become happy and prosperous, <reference osisRef="Job.11.12-Job.11.20">Job 11:12-20</reference>. <div eID="gen16330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16331" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16332" type="x-p"/> Zophar the Naamathite - Of this man and his friends, see <reference osisRef="Job.2.11">Job 2:11</reference>. He is the most inveterate of Job's accusers, and generally speaks without feeling or pity. In sour godliness he excelled all the rest. This chapter and the twentieth comprehends all that he said. He was too crooked to speak much in measured verse.
entries.032cd58e7e45325c91d293b35c6db5fd825f8a73: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16333" type="x-p"/> Should not the multitude of words be answered? - Some translate, "To multiply words profiteth nothing." <div eID="gen16333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16334" type="x-p"/> And should a man full of talk be justified - איש שפתים ish sephathayim, "a man of lips," a proper appellation for a great talker: he is "a man of lips," i.e., his lips are the only active parts of his system.
entries.db3a00157f880983d0fe11dfd0b869662ca59f1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16335" type="x-p"/> Should thy lies make men hold their peace? - This is a very severe reproof, and not justified by the occasion. <div eID="gen16335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16336" type="x-p"/> And when thou mockest - As thou despisest others, shall no man put thee to scorn? Zophar could never think that the solemn and awful manner in which Job spoke could be called bubbling, as some would translate the term לעג laag. He might consider Job's speech as sarcastic and severe, but he could not consider it as nonsense.
entries.232409dd29cf2dee3f5a2d6f0c77eeff93af1079: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16337" type="x-p"/> My doctrine is pure - לקחי likchi, "my assumptions." What I assume or take as right, and just, and true, are so; the precepts which I have formed, and the practice which I have founded on them, are all correct and perfect. Job had not exactly said, My doctrine and way of life are pure, and I am clean in thine eyes; but he had vindicated himself from their charges of secret sins and hypocrisy, and appealed to God for his general uprightness and sincerity: but Zophar here begs the question, in order that he may have something to say, and room to give vent to his invective.
entries.a363d98f29c14225cc3cb72b1edacb20e9f480bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16338" type="x-p"/> But O that God would speak - How little feeling, humanity, and charity is there in this prayer!
entries.28dc3c1a270623fb2cdb0003fd5ffc61e6bc5b37: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16339" type="x-p"/> The secrets of wisdom - All the depths of his own counsels; the heights, lengths, and breadths, of holiness. That they are double to that which is, תושיה tushiyah, which we translate that which is, is a word frequent in Job and in the Book of Proverbs, and is one of the evidences brought in favor of Solomon as the author of this book. It signifies substance or essence, and is translated by a great variety of terms; enterprise, completeness, substance, the whole constitution, wisdom, law, sound wisdom, solid complete happiness, solidity of reason and truth, the complete total sum, etc., etc. See Taylor's Hebrew and English Concord., under ישה. In this place the versions are various. Coverdale, following the Vulgate, translates: That he might shewe the (out of his secrite wissdome) how manyfolde his lawe is. The Septuagint, ὁτι διπλους εσται των κατα σε, that it is double to what it is with thee. Mr. Good translates, "For they are intricacies to Iniquity." This is a meaning never before given to תושיה tushiyah, and a meaning which even his own learned note will not make generally prevalent. Perhaps Zophar is here, in mind, comparing the wisdom which has been revealed with the wisdom not revealed. The perfection and excellence of the Divine nature and the purity of his law, are, in substance and essence, double or manifold to the revelation already made. <div eID="gen16339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16340" type="x-p"/> Less than thine iniquity deserveth - Mr. Good translates, And the knowledge hath withdrawn from thee because of thy sins; and represents Zophar as praying that God would reveal to him the secrets of wisdom, and the knowledge which he had withdrawn from him because of his transgressions. That Zophar intends to insinuate that God afflicted Job because of his iniquities, is evident; and that he thought that God had inflicted less chastisement upon him than his sins deserved, is not less so; and that, therefore, Job's complaining of harsh treatment was not at all well founded.
entries.4cf086cf12e1ae1559b999971af792eb684be177: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16341" type="x-p"/> Canst thou by searching find out God? - What is God? A Being self-existent, eternal, infinite, immense, without bounds, incomprehensible either by mind, or time, or space. Who then can find this Being out? Who can fathom his depths, ascend to his heights, extend to his breadths, and comprehend the infinitude of his perfections?
entries.07cf6ab24d2992b3e821e96fc6cc0e95d6bb16a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16342" type="x-p"/> It is as high as heaven - High as the heavens, what canst thou work? Deep below sheol, (the invisible world), what canst thou know? Long beyond the earth, and broad beyond the sea, is its measure. These are instances in the immensity of created things, and all out of the reach of human power and knowledge; and if these things are so, how incomprehensible must he be, who designed, created, preserves, and governs the whole! <div eID="gen16342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16343" type="x-p"/> We find the same thought in Milton: - "These are thy glorious works, Parent of good! <div eID="gen16343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16344" type="x-p"/> Almighty! Thine this universal frame: <div eID="gen16344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16345" type="x-p"/> How wondrous fair! Thyself how wondrous then!"
entries.98bc1191f5c662fc1f74ac60cd1690b4ac7bf2b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16346" type="x-p"/> If he cut off - As he is unlimited and almighty, he cannot be controlled. He will do whatsoever he pleases; and he is pleased with nothing but what is right. Who then will dare to find fault? Perhaps Zophar may refer to Job's former state, his losses and afflictions. If he cut off, as he has done, thy children; if he shut up, as he has done, thyself by this sore disease; or gather together hostile bands to invade thy territories and carry away thy property; who can hinder him? He is sovereign, and has a right to dispose of his own property as he pleases.
entries.6dca386f04947a44a71829ee84ccc501ad05a8f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16347" type="x-p"/> He knoweth vain men - מתי שוא methey shau, "men of falsehood." <div eID="gen16347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16348" type="x-p"/> He seeth wickedness - He sees as well what is in man, as what man does; and of his actions and propensities he cannot be an indifferent spectator.
entries.d2b7f6109df5c8a3b92677a8cb51d0c1f3998c6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16349" type="x-p"/> For vain man would be wise - The original is difficult and uncertain, ואיש נבוב ילבב veish nabub yillabeb, "And shall the hollow man assume courage," or "pride himself?" Or, as Mr. Good rather paraphrases it, Will he then accept the hollow-hearted person? The Chaldee gives two renderings: An eloquent man shall become wiser in his heart, and the colt of the wild ass is born as the son of man. Or, The wise man shall ponder it; and the refractory youth, who at last becomes prudent, shall make a great man. Coverdale - A vayne body exalteth him self; and the son of man is like a wylde asse's foale. Houbigant translates thus: - A man who hath understanding will become prudent; but he who is as the wild ass hath no heart, i.e., sense. According to this critic, the meaning is this: - A man of sense, should he at any time transgress, will learn wisdom from it; but a man of a brutish mind, uncultivated and unreflecting, will plunge yet deeper into iniquity. <div eID="gen16349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16350" type="x-p"/> Though man be born like a wild ass's colt - Is translated by Mr. Good, Or shall the wild ass colt assume the man? This is making a sense, but such as I fear the original will never allow. There is no end to the translations of this verse, and conjectures relative to its meaning. I shall conclude with the Vulgate - Vir vanus in superbiam erigitur, et tanquam pullum onagri se liberum natum putat, "Vain man is puffed up with pride; and he supposes himself to be born free like the wild ass's colt." Man is full of self-conceit; and imagines himself born to act as he pleases, to roam at large, to be under no control, and to be accountable to none for his actions.
entries.b730aba768331eb8e0965dc63a2aa2ec0113d32e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16351" type="x-p"/> If thou prepare thine heart - Make use of the powers which God has given thee, and be determined to seek him with all thy soul. <div eID="gen16351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16352" type="x-p"/> And stretch out thine hands toward him - Making fervent prayer and supplication, putting away iniquity out of thy hand, and not permitting wickedness to dwell in thy tabernacle; then thou shalt lift up thy face without a blush, thou wilt become established, and have nothing to fear, <reference osisRef="Job.11.14">Job 11:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>. <div eID="gen16352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16353" type="x-p"/> There is a sentiment in <reference osisRef="Pro.16.1">Pro 16:1</reference>, very similar to that in the <reference osisRef="Job.11.13">Job 11:13</reference>, which we translate very improperly: - לאדם מערכי לב leadam maarchey leb. <div eID="gen16353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16354" type="x-p"/> To man are the preparations of the heart: ומהוה מענה לשון umeyehovah maaneh lashon. <div eID="gen16354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16355" type="x-p"/> But from Jehovah is the answer to the tongue. <div eID="gen16355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16356" type="x-p"/> It is man's duty to pray; it is God's prerogative to answer. Zophar, like all the rest, is true to his principle. Job must be a wicked man, else he had not been afflicted. There must be some iniquity in his hand, and some wickedness tolerated in his family. So they all supposed.
entries.8ae83f97f1e9611c0d85d1f4aa36d8aee1588c94: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16357" type="x-p"/> Because thou shalt forget thy misery - Thou shalt have such long and complete rest, that thou shalt scarcely remember thy labor. <div eID="gen16357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16358" type="x-p"/> As waters that pass away - Like as the mountain floods, which sweep every thing before them, houses, tents, cattle, and the produce of the field, and are speedily absorbed by the sandy plains over which they run, so shalt thou remember thy sufferings: they were wasting and ruinous for the time, but were soon over and gone.
entries.22e933dba8886a1ff816526b94b41e01cb335c77: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16359" type="x-p"/> Thine age shall be clearer than the noonday - The rest of thy life shall be unclouded prosperity. <div eID="gen16359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16360" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt shine forth - Thou shalt be in this unclouded state, as the sun in the firmament of heaven, giving light and heat to all around thee. <div eID="gen16360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16361" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt be as the morning - Thus the sun of thy prosperity shall arise, and shine more and more unto the perfect day. This is the image which the sacred writer employs, and it is correct and elegant.
entries.c0f11cd9c196a0d10385ffa39d51d0edbcaaacf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16362" type="x-p"/> And thou shalt be secure - Thou shalt not fear any farther evils to disturb thy prosperity, for thou shalt have a well-grounded hope and confidence that thou shalt no more be visited by adversity. <div eID="gen16362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16363" type="x-p"/> Yea, thou shalt dig - I believe this neither refers to digging his grave, nor to curiously investigating surrounding circumstances; but to the custom of digging for water in the places where they pitched their tents. It was a matter of high importance in Asiatic countries to find good wells of wholesome water; and they were frequently causes of contention among neighboring chiefs, who sometimes stopped them up, and at other times seized them as their own. Through envy of Isaac's prosperity the Philistines stopped up all the wells which Abraham had digged, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.12-Gen.26.16">Gen 26:12-16</reference>. And we find the herdsmen of Gerar contending with Isaac's servants about the wells which the latter had digged; so that they were obliged to abandon two of the chief of them, and remove to a distance in order to dig and find quiet possession. See <reference osisRef="Gen.31.17-Gen.31.22">Gen 31:17-22</reference>. Zophar, in reference to all these sorts of contentions and petty wars about wells and springs, tells Job that in the state of prosperity to which he shall be brought by the good providence of God, he shall dig - find wells of living water; none shall contend with him; and he shall rest in safety, all the neighboring chieftains cultivating friendship with him; see on <reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job 5:23</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Job.5.24">Job 5:24</reference> (note); and that this is the meaning of the passage the following verse shows: Thou shalt lie down, and none shall make thee afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thee. Thou shalt be in perfect security; no enemy shall molest thee, and many shall seek thy friendship.
entries.b4176284183a72d7ee36fab14b87743c50978661: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16364" type="x-p"/> The eyes of the wicked shall fail - They shall be continually looking out for help and deliverance; but their expectation shall be cut off. <div eID="gen16364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16365" type="x-p"/> And they shall not escape - They shall receive the punishment due to their deserts; for God has his eye continually upon them. מנהם ומנוס אבד umanos abad minnehem, literally, "And escape perishes from them." Flight from impending destruction is impossible. <div eID="gen16365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16366" type="x-p"/> And their hope shall be as the giving up of the ghost - ותקותם מפח נפש vethikratham mappach naphesh, "And their hope an exhalation of breath," or a mere wish of the mind. They retain their hope to the last; and the last breath they breathe is the final and eternal termination of their hope. They give up their hope and their ghost together; for a vain hope cannot enter into that place where shadow and representation exist not; all being substance and reality. And thus endeth Zophar the Naamathite; whose premises were in general good, his conclusions legitimate, but his application of them to Job's case totally erroneous; because he still proceeded on the ground that Job was a wicked man, if not ostensibly, yet secretly; and that the sufferings he was undergoing were the means by which God was unmasking him to the view of men. But, allowing that Job had been a bad man, the exhortations of Zophar were well calculated to enforce repentance and excite confidence in the Divine mercy. Zophar seems to have had a full conviction of the all-governing providence of God; and that those who served him with an honest and upright heart would be ever distinguished in the distribution of temporal good. He seems however to think that rewards and punishments were distributed in this life, and does not refer, at least very evidently, to a future state. Probably his information on subjects of divinity did not extend much beyond the grave; and we have much cause to thank God for a clearer dispensation. Deus nobis haec otia fecit. God grant that we may make a good use of it!  <chapter eID="Job.11"/> <div eID="gen16366" type="x-p"/>

entries.737b0daae20cbf7922ed7931f2195f8f691d41fa: <reference osisRef="Job.11.1-Job.6.1">Job 11:1-6   1</reference>  Then began Zophar the Naamathite, and said:   2  Shall the torrent of words remain unanswered, <div eID="gen7268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7269" type="x-p"/> And shall the prater be in the right?   3  Shall thy vain talking silence the people, <div eID="gen7269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7270" type="x-p"/> So that thou mockest without any one putting thee to shame,   4  And sayest: my doctrine is pure, <div eID="gen7270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7271" type="x-p"/> And I am guiltless in Thine eyes?   5  But oh that Eloah would speak, <div eID="gen7271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7272" type="x-p"/> And open His lips against thee,   6  And make known to thee the secrets of wisdom, <div eID="gen7272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7273" type="x-p"/> That she is twofold in her nature - <div eID="gen7273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7274" type="x-p"/> Know then that Eloah forgetteth much of thy guilt. <div eID="gen7274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7275" type="x-p"/> When Job has concluded his long speech, Zophar, the third and most impetuous of the friends, begins. His name, if it is to be explained according to the Arabic Esauitish name <hi type="italic">el - assfar</hi>,<note placement="foot">Vid., Abulfeda’s <hi type="italic">Historia anteislamica ed. Fleischer</hi>, p. 168.</note> signifies the yellow one (<hi type="italic">flavedo</hi>), and the name of the place whence he comes, pleasantness (<hi type="italic">amaenitas</hi>). The very beginning of his speech is impassioned. He calls Job’s speech דברים רב, a multitude of words (besides here, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">Pro 10:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Ecc 5:2</reference>), and asks whether he is to remain unanswered; יענה לא, <hi type="italic">responsum non feret</hi>, from נענה, not the sense of being humbled, but: to be answered (of the suppliant: to be heard = to receive an answer). He calls Job שׂפתים אישׁ, a prater (distinct from דברים איש, a ready speaker, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.10">Exo 4:10</reference>), who is not in the right, whom one must not allow to have the last word. The questions, <reference osisRef="Job.11.2">Job 11:2</reference>, are followed by another which is not denoted by the sign of a question, but is only known by the accent: Shall not thy בּדּים, meaningless speeches (from בדד = בטא, βαττολογεῖν), put men (מתים, like other archaisms, e.g., תּבל, always without the article) to silence, so that thou darest mock without any one making thee ashamed, i.e., leading thee on <hi type="italic">ad absurdum?</hi> Thou darest mock <hi type="italic">God</hi> (Hirzel); better Rosenmüller: <hi type="italic">nos et Deum.</hi> The mockery here meant is that which Zophar has heard in Job’s long speech; mockery at his opponents, in the belief that he is right because they remain silent. The <hi type="italic">futt. consec.,</hi> Job 11:3., describe the conduct of Job which results from this absence of contradiction. Zophar, in v. 4, does not take up Job’s own words, but means, that one had better have nothing more to do with Job, as he would some day say and think so and so, he would consider his doctrine blameless, and himself in relation to God pure. לקח occurs only here in this book; it is a word peculiar to the book of Proverbs (also only <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">Deu 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.24">Isa 29:24</reference>), and properly signifies the act of appropriating, then that which is presented for appropriation, i.e., for learning: the doctrine (similar to שׁמועה, the hearing, ἀκοή, and then the discourse); we see from the words “my doctrine is pure,” which Zophar puts into the mouth of Job, that the controversy becomes more and more a controversy respecting known principles.
entries.c0e191c5cb7a480421ec83033d79d8ecc8a217b5: <reference osisRef="Job.11.7-Job.9.7">Job 11:7-9   7</reference>  Canst thou find out the nature of Eloah, <div eID="gen7276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7277" type="x-p"/> And penetrate to the foundation of the existence of the Almighty?   8  It is as the heights of heaven-what wilt thou do? <div eID="gen7277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7278" type="x-p"/> Deeper than Hades-what canst thou know?   9  The measure thereof is longer than the earth, <div eID="gen7278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7279" type="x-p"/> And broader than the sea. <div eID="gen7279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7280" type="x-p"/> The majority of modern commentators erroneously translate חקר searching = comprehension, and תּכלית perfection, a meaning which this word never has. The former, indeed, signifies first in an active sense: finding out by search; and then also objectively: the object sought after: “the hidden ground” (Ewald), the depth (here and <reference osisRef="Job.38.16">Job 38:16</reference>; also, according to Ew., <reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>, of the deep innermost thought). The latter denotes penetrating to the extreme, and then the extreme, πέρας, itself (<reference osisRef="Job.26.10">Job 26:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.3">Job 28:3</reference>). In other words: the nature that underlies that which is visible as an object of search is called חקר; and the extreme of a thing, i.e., the end, without which the beginning and middle cannot be understood, is called תכלית. The nature of God may be sought after, but cannot be found out; and the end of God is unattainable, for He is both: the Perfect One, <hi type="italic">absolutus</hi>; and the Endless One, <hi type="italic">infinitus</hi>.
entries.8a967988cc6211d4561925961dcf56b618d708c7: <reference osisRef="Job.11.10-Job.12.10">Job 11:10-12 10</reference>  When He passes by and arrests <div eID="gen7281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7282" type="x-p"/> And calls to judgment, who will oppose Him? 11  For He knoweth the men devoid of principle, <div eID="gen7282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7283" type="x-p"/> And seeth wickedness without observing it. 12  But before an empty head gaineth understanding, <div eID="gen7283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7284" type="x-p"/> A wild ass would become a man. <div eID="gen7284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7285" type="x-p"/> In יחלף God is conceived as one who manifests himself by passing to and fro in the powers of nature (in the whirlwind, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Isa 21:1</reference>). Should He meet with one who is guilty, and seize and bring him to judgment, who then (<hi type="italic">waw apod.</hi>) will turn Him back, i.e., restrain Him? הקהיל is used of bringing to judgment, with reference to the ancient form of trial which was in public, and in which the carrying out of the sentence was partly incumbent on the people (1Ki 21:9; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.40">Eze 16:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.46">Eze 23:46</reference>). One might almost imagine that Zophar looks upon himself and the other two friends as forming such an “assembly:” they cannot justify him in opposition to God, since He accounts him guilty. God’s mode of trial is summary, because infallible: He knows altogether שׁוא מתי, people who hypocritically disguise their moral nothingness (on this idea, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.26.4">Psa 26:4</reference>); and sees (looks through) און (from the root <hi type="italic">ân</hi>, to breathe), otherwise grief, with which one pants, in a moral sense worthlessness, without any trace whatever of worth or substance. He knows and sees this moral wretchedness at once, and need not first of all reflect upon it: <hi type="italic">non opus habet,</hi> as Abenezra has correctly explained, <hi type="italic">ut diu consideret</hi> (comp. the like thought, <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>). <div eID="gen7285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7286" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference> has been variously misinterpreted. Gesenius in his <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi><note placement="foot">Vid., Lexicon, Engl. edition, s.v. לבב Niphal. - Tr.</note> translates: but man is empty and void of understanding; but this is contrary to the accentuation, according to which נבוב אישׁ together form the subject. Olshausen translates better: an empty man, on the other hand, is without heart; but the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. cannot be exactly so used, and if we consider that <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> has never properly a privative meaning, though sometimes a privative idea (as e.g., סקּל, <hi type="italic">operam consumere in lapidos, scil. ejiciendos</hi>), we must regard a privative <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> as likewise inadmissible. Stickel translates peculiarly: the man devoid of understanding is enraged against God; but this is opposed to the manifest correlation of נבוב and ילּבב, which does not indicate the antithesis of an empty and sulky person (Böttcher): the former rather signifies empty, and the latter to acquire heart or marrow (Heidenheim, לב יקנה), so that לב fills up the hollow space. Hirzel’s rendering partly bears out the requirement of this correlation: man has understanding like a hollow pate; but this explanation, like that of Gesenius, violates the accentuation, and produces an affected witticism. The explanation which regards <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference> as descriptive of the wholesome effect of the discipline of the divine judgments (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference>) is far better; it does not violate the accent, and moreover is more in accordance with the future form: the empty one becomes discerning thereby, the rough, humane (thus recently Ewald, Heiligst., Schlottm.); but according to this explanation, <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference> is not connected with what immediately precedes, nor is the peculiarity of the expression fully brought out. Hupfeld opens up another way of interpreting the passage when he remarks, <hi type="italic">nil dicto facilius et simplicius;</hi> he understands <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference></hi> according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference></hi>: But man is furnished with an empty heart, i.e., receives at his birth an empty undiscerning heart, and man is born as a wild ass’s colt, i.e., as stupid and obstinate. This thought is satisfactorily connected with the preceding; but here also נבוב is taken as predicate in violation of the accentuation, nor is justice done to the correlation above referred to, and the whole sentence is referred to the portion of man at his birth, in opposition to the impression conveyed by the use of the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. Oehler appears to us to have recognised the right sense: But an empty man is as little endowed with sense, as that a wild ass should ever be born as man - be, so to speak, born again and become a man.<note placement="foot">Wetzstein explains: “But a man that barks like a dog (i.e., rages shamelessly) can become sensible, and a young wild ass (i.e., the wildest and roughest creature) be born again as a man (i.e., become gentle and civilised),” from נבב = נבח, since נבח is the commoner word for “barking” in the Syrian towns and villages, and נבב, on the other hand, is used among those who dwelt in tents. But we must then point it נבּוּב, and the antithesis ילּבב is more favourable the Hebrew meaning, “hollowed out, empty.”</note> <div eID="gen7286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7287" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">waw</hi> in ועיר is just like <reference osisRef="Job.5.7">Job 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.11">Job 12:11</reference>, and brings into close connection the things that are to be compared, as in the form of emblematic proverbs (vid., Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real Encyklopädie</hi>, xiv. 696): the one will happen not earlier than, and as little as, the other. The <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> נולד, which in <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pro 17:17</reference> signifies to become manifest, here borders on the notion of <hi type="italic">regenerari</hi>; a regeneration would be necessary if the wild ass should become human, - a regeneration which is inconceivable. It is by nature refractory, and especially when young (ועיר from Arab. <hi type="italic">‛âr , fut.</hi> <hi type="italic">i</hi> in the signification <hi type="italic">vagari</hi>, <hi type="italic">huc illuc discurrere,</hi> of a young, restless, wild, frisking animal). Just so, says Zophar, the vacuum in an empty man is incapable of being filled up, - a side hit at Job, which rebounds on Zophar himself; for the dogma of the friends, which forms the sole contents of their hollowness, can indeed not fill with brightness and peace a heart that is passing through conflict. The peculiarity of the expression is no longer unintelligible; Zophar is the most impassioned of the three friends.
entries.686015082b261c037ab307aaca4a178c58f5d173: Job 11:13-15 13  But if thou wilt direct thy heart, <div eID="gen7287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7288" type="x-p"/> And spread out thy hands to Him - 14  If there is evil in thy hand, put it far away, <div eID="gen7288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7289" type="x-p"/> And let not wickedness dwell in thy tents - 15  Then indeed canst thou lift up thy face without spot, <div eID="gen7289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7290" type="x-p"/> And shalt be firm without fearing. <div eID="gen7290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7291" type="x-p"/> The phrase הכין לב signifies neither to raise the heart (Ewald), nor to establish it (Hirz.), but to direct it, i.e., give it the right direction (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.8">Psa 78:8</reference>) towards God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">1Sa 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.33">2Ch 20:33</reference>; it has an independent meaning, so that there is no need to supply אל־אל, nor take וּפרשׂתּ to be for לפרושׂ (after the construction in <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.19">2Ch 30:19</reference>). To spread out the hands in prayer is כּפּים (פּרשׂ) פּרשׂ; ידים is seldom used instead of the more artistic כפים, <hi type="italic">palmas, h.e. manus supinas.</hi> The conditional antecedent clause is immediately followed, <reference osisRef="Job.11.14">Job 11:14</reference>, by a similarly conditional parenthetical clause, which inserts the indispensable condition of acceptable prayer; the conclusion might begin with הרהיקהוּ: when thou sendest forth thy heart and spreadest out thy hands to Him, if there is wickedness in thy hand, put it far away; but the antecedent requires a promise for its conclusion, and the more so since the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. and <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. which follow אם, <reference osisRef="Job.11.13">Job 11:13</reference>, have the force of <hi type="italic">futt. exact.:</hi> <hi type="italic">si disposueris et extenderis,</hi> to which the conclusion: put it far away, is not suited, which rather expresses a preliminary condition of acceptable prayer.
